scope.title: Conventional AM, envelope and modulation index

research.governingQuestion: How does the envelope of conventional AM carry the message, how is the modulation index measured, and why does mu>1 break envelope detection?

sources.label: University of Ottawa ELG3175 Introduction to Communication Systems: Conventional AM (lecture slides)
University of Maryland, Tretter: Chapter 5 Amplitude Modulation (lab course slides)
Kiki analog-modulation ledger notation (mu, Ac, fm, fc) and lab route

claims.text: Single-tone conventional AM is s(t)=Ac[1+mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)]cos(2*pi*fc*t), with modulation index mu.
claims.check: S-2 slide 5-3 gives s(t)=Ac(1+mu cos wm t)cos wc t with mu=ka*Am; S-1 slide 4 defines ma=ka*mp.

claims.text: The envelope Ac[1+mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)] is the smooth curve through the positive peaks of s(t) when fc is much larger than the message bandwidth.
claims.check: S-2 slide 5-2; S-1 slide 7 names Ac[1+ka m(t)] the envelope.

claims.text: For 0<=mu<=1, Emax=Ac(1+mu) and Emin=Ac(1-mu), so mu=(Emax-Emin)/(Emax+Emin).
claims.check: S-2 slide 5-4 gives mu=(1-emin/emax)/(1+emin/emax); multiplying by emax gives (Emax-Emin)/(Emax+Emin). Derived: (Ac(1+mu)-Ac(1-mu))/(Ac(1+mu)+Ac(1-mu))=2Ac*mu/2Ac=mu.

claims.text: At mu=1 the envelope periodically reaches zero (100% modulation); mu>1 is overmodulation.
An overmodulated AM signal cannot be recovered with the noncoherent envelope-detection method; recovery needs the envelope to stay non-negative.
claims.check: S-1 slide 8; S-2 slide 5-2 (envelope must be >= 0 for recovery).

claims.text: The transmitted signal contains a carrier term, which carries no message information, plus two sidebands of amplitude 0.5*Ac*mu.
A half-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter is a simple envelope detector when fc is much larger than the message bandwidth.
With Emax=6 V and Emin=2 V, mu=(6-2)/(6+2)=0.5 (50% modulation).
Emax+Emin=2Ac, so Ac=(Emax+Emin)/2; for 9 V and 3 V, Ac=6 V.
claims.check: derived from CL-3: Ac(1+mu)+Ac(1-mu)=2Ac; (9+3)/2=6. Also mu=(9-3)/(9+3)=0.5.

claims.text: The envelope detector output is approximately Ac+Ac*mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t); blocking DC leaves the message term.
claims.check: S-1 slide 20 (Ac+Ac ka m(t), DC blocked by a transformer). Worked example check: Emax=5 V, Emin=1 V gives mu=4/6=0.67; example 8 V/2 V gives 6/10=0.6.

claims.text: Kiki uses mu for the AM modulation index and Ac, fm, fc for carrier amplitude, message and carrier frequency.
claims.check: Matches the existing ledger and saved canvas controls; S-1 writes ma and ka.

openQuestions: S-3 earlier cited a MathWorks page for mu and overmodulation; that page (checked 2026-11-20) covers DSB AM with an offset k, not the modulation index. Replace that citation in the ledger.

learner.troublesome: Students must hold the carrier, the envelope and the message apart at once, and the envelope is the message plus a constant, not the message itself. The mu=1 boundary is counter-intuitive: more modulation sounds better until it breaks detection.

misconceptions.statement: A larger modulation index is always better; mu above 1 just makes the message stronger.
misconceptions.correction: Above mu=1 the envelope crosses zero, so an envelope detector output becomes distorted.
misconceptions.reasoning: Students generalise 'more modulation = louder'. S-2 Experiment 5.1 has students raise the input until overmodulation to observe this effect, which implies it must be confronted.

misconceptions.statement: The envelope is the message signal itself.
misconceptions.correction: The envelope is the message shifted up by the constant carrier level Ac and scaled; DC must be removed to get the message.
misconceptions.reasoning: S-1 slide 20 needs an explicit DC-blocking step, a step students skip when they equate envelope and message.

teaching.canDo: Read Emax and Emin from an AM trace, calculate mu, and say whether an envelope detector will recover the message.
teaching.keyIdea: The envelope Ac(1+mu*cos) carries the message only while 0<=mu<=1; beyond that, overmodulation breaks envelope detection.

explanation.text: Conventional AM keeps the carrier and lets the carrier amplitude follow the message. The envelope is the smooth outline through the positive peaks of the waveform. For a single tone it is Ac(1+mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)), so it rises and falls with the message but also sits on the constant level Ac. When 0<=mu<=1 the envelope never falls below zero, and a simple envelope detector recovers the message. When mu>1 the envelope crosses zero: this is overmodulation, and the detector output is distorted. From an oscilloscope trace, mu=(Emax-Emin)/(Emax+Emin).

walkthrough.target: smooth outline through the positive peaks
walkthrough.say: The envelope is the outline you would trace by joining the positive peaks of the waveform.
The envelope sits on the constant level Ac, so it is the message shifted up, not the message itself.
Overmodulation means mu is greater than one, so the envelope crosses zero and a simple detector cannot follow the message.
Read the largest and smallest envelope values from the trace and use mu=(Emax-Emin)/(Emax+Emin).

example.title: Checking a transmitter on the oscilloscope
example.scenario: A lab AM transmitter shows an envelope that swings between 8 V and 2 V on the oscilloscope.
example.takeaway: mu=(8-2)/(8+2)=0.6, safely below 1, so an envelope detector will work.

checks.prompt: An AM envelope has Emax=6 V and Emin=2 V. What is mu?
checks.explanation: mu=(6-2)/(6+2)=4/8=0.5. Dividing by Emax alone gives 0.67; the ratio needs Emax+Emin because the envelope swings both above and below Ac.

checks.prompt: Which modulation index makes single-tone conventional AM overmodulated?

distractorRationale.0.4: error: confuses shallow modulation with distortion
distractorRationale.0.8: error: thinks values close to 1 are already overmodulated

checks.explanation: Overmodulation needs mu>1, so only 1.3 makes the envelope cross zero. At mu=1.0 the envelope just touches zero: that is 100% modulation, not overmodulation.

checks.prompt: A student raises mu from 0.8 to 1.4 to get a stronger message from an envelope detector. What happens?
options: The detected message becomes cleaner and louder
Nothing changes, because the carrier frequency is the same
The carrier disappears from the transmitted signal

distractorRationale.Nothing changes, because the carrier fre: error: thinks only frequency affects detection
distractorRationale.The carrier disappears from the transmit: error: confuses overmodulation with suppressed-carrier modulation

checks.explanation: At mu=1.4 the envelope crosses zero, so the detector cannot follow it and the output is distorted. A larger mu helps only up to mu=1.

checks.prompt: The envelope of a single-tone AM signal swings between 9 V and 3 V. What is the carrier amplitude Ac?

distractorRationale.9 V: error: took the peak Emax as Ac
distractorRationale.12 V: error: added Emax and Emin without halving

checks.explanation: Emax=Ac(1+mu) and Emin=Ac(1-mu), so Emax+Emin=2Ac and Ac=(9+3)/2=6 V. Taking the 9 V peak as Ac forgets that the envelope rises above the carrier level.

checks.prompt: Why does a receiver pass the envelope detector output Ac+Ac*mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t) through a DC-blocking stage?
options: To remove the carrier frequency fc from the output
To remove the constant level Ac and keep only the message variation
To reduce mu below 1 after detection
To restore a carrier that was suppressed
checks.answer: To remove the constant level Ac and keep only the message variation

distractorRationale.To remove the carrier frequency fc from: error: confuses the RC ripple filter with DC blocking
distractorRationale.To reduce mu below 1 after detection: error: believes later stages can undo overmodulation
distractorRationale.To restore a carrier that was suppressed: error: confuses conventional AM with suppressed-carrier AM

checks.explanation: The envelope is the message plus the constant Ac, not the message itself. Blocking DC removes Ac and leaves Ac*mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t); the RC filter, not the DC block, removes the fc ripple.

checks.prompt: In one or two English sentences, explain why an envelope detector cannot recover the message when mu>1.
checks.answer: When mu>1 the envelope Ac(1+mu*cos) becomes negative for part of each cycle, so the detector, which follows only the positive peaks, no longer traces the message and the output is distorted.

checks.prompt: In the simulator you change mu from 0.5 to 1.2 and view the envelope. Predict what you will see and why.
checks.answer: The envelope will cross zero and the detected output will be distorted, because Ac(1+mu*cos) becomes negative when mu>1.
